p.src: Now Zhang Fei, because Lord Guan had released the waters upstream, led his troops in an attack from downstream, intercepted Cao Ren, and fell upon his disordered ranks. Suddenly he encountered Xu Chu and engaged him in combat. Xu Chu dared not prolong the fight and forced his way out to escape. Zhang Fei pursued him, then joined Xuande and Kongming, and together they followed the river upstream. Liu Feng and Mi Fang had already prepared boats and were waiting; all crossed the river together and made straight for Fancheng. Kongming ordered the boats and rafts set afire and destroyed.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Ren gathered his surviving troops and encamped at Xinye, then sent Cao Hong to report the defeat fully to Cao Cao. Cao Cao flew into a rage. “How dare that village rustic Zhuge treat me so!” He drove the three armies onward, covering hills and choking fields, until all reached Xinye and made camp. He ordered the soldiers to scour the hills while filling in the White River. Then he divided the great army into eight columns and sent them all against Fancheng. Liu Ye said, “Prime Minister, having only just arrived at Xiangyang, you must first win the people’s hearts. Liu Bei has now moved all the people of Xinye into Fancheng. If our troops advance directly, both cities will be ground to dust. It would be better first to send someone to summon Liu Bei to surrender. Even if Bei refuses, it will still show that we cherish the people. If he does surrender, the lands of Jingzhou may be pacified without a battle.”

p.src: Cao Cao accepted his counsel and asked, “Who can serve as envoy?” Liu Ye replied, “Xu Shu is deeply attached to Liu Bei and is now in our army. Why not order him to go?” Cao Cao said, “I fear that once he goes, he will not return.” Liu Ye said, “If he does not return, he will make himself a laughingstock. Have no doubts, Prime Minister.” Cao Cao therefore summoned Xu Shu and said, “I intend now to level Fancheng, yet I pity the lives of its many people. You may go and persuade Liu Bei: if he will surrender, his offenses shall be pardoned and he shall receive a noble rank. If he persists in his delusion, soldiers and civilians alike shall be slaughtered, jade and common stone burned together. I know your loyalty and honor, and therefore send you especially. I trust you will not fail me.”

p.src: Xu Shu accepted the command and went to Fancheng. Xuande and Kongming received him, and together they spoke of their friendship in former days. Xu Shu said, “Cao Cao sent me to summon you to surrender, my lord, but this is only a pretense to win the people’s hearts. He has divided his troops into eight columns and is advancing after filling in the White River. I fear Fancheng cannot be held; you should swiftly make plans to depart.” Xuande wished to keep Xu Shu with him. Xu Shu declined, saying, “If I do not return, I fear I shall invite the world’s ridicule. Now that my aged mother is dead, I shall bear lifelong remorse. Though my body remains with him, I swear never to devise a single stratagem for him. With Sleeping Dragon to assist you, why fear that your great enterprise will not succeed? I beg leave to depart.” Xuande dared not compel him to stay.

p.src: Xu Shu took his leave and returned. On seeing Cao Cao, he reported that Xuande had no intention of surrendering. Cao Cao was furious and advanced his army that very day. Xuande asked Kongming for a plan. Kongming said, “We should swiftly abandon Fancheng and go to Xiangyang to rest for a time.” Xuande said, “But the people have followed me so long. How could I bear to abandon them?” Kongming said, “Have it proclaimed everywhere that those who wish may come with us, while those unwilling may remain.” First he sent Yun-chang to the riverbank to put the boats in order, then ordered Sun Qian and Jian Yong to proclaim throughout the city: “Cao Cao’s troops will soon arrive. This isolated city cannot long be defended. Any of the people who wish to follow may cross the river with us.”

p.src: The people of both counties cried out with one voice, “Though we die, we are willing to follow you, my lord!” That very day they set out, wailing and weeping. Supporting the old and carrying the young, men and women bringing one another along, they streamed endlessly across the river while cries of grief never ceased on either bank. Seeing this from his boat, Xuande grieved bitterly and cried, “That the people should suffer this great calamity for me alone! What right have I to live?” He tried to throw himself into the river and die, but those around him hastily restrained him. All who heard him wept bitterly. When his boat reached the southern bank, he looked back at the people; those who had not yet crossed faced south and wept. Xuande urgently ordered Yun-chang to hasten the boats and ferry them over; only then did he mount his horse. When they reached Xiangyang’s eastern gate, they saw banners planted all along the walls and chevaux-de-frise thickly arrayed beside the moat. Xuande reined in his horse and called loudly, “My worthy nephew Liu Cong, I wish only to save the people and have no other design. Open the gate at once!”

p.src: When Liu Cong heard that Xuande had arrived, he was afraid and would not come out. Cai Mao and Zhang Yun went straight to the gate tower and angrily ordered the soldiers to shoot down a hail of arrows. The people outside the city all faced the gate tower and wept. Suddenly, an officer inside the city led several hundred men directly onto the tower and shouted, “Cai Mao and Zhang Yun, you traitorous villains! Lord Liu is a man of benevolence and virtue. He has now come seeking refuge in order to save the people. How dare you refuse him!” All looked upon the man: he stood eight chi tall, and his face was the color of a ripe jujube. He was a native of Yiyang, surnamed Wei, named Yan, with the style Wenchang.

p.src: At once Wei Yan whirled his blade, cut down the officers guarding the gate, opened it, and lowered the drawbridge. He shouted, “Imperial Uncle Liu, quickly lead your troops into the city, and let us slay the traitors together!” Zhang Fei immediately spurred his horse forward to enter. Xuande hastily stopped him, saying, “Do not alarm the people!” Wei Yan continued calling Xuande’s troops into the city. Then an officer within the city galloped out at the head of his troops and shouted, “Wei Yan, you nameless foot soldier! How dare you raise a revolt! Do you recognize me, the great general Wen Ping?” Wei Yan was enraged. Leveling his spear, he spurred his horse forward to fight.

p.src: The soldiers of both sides fought chaotically beside the city, their battle cries shaking the air. Xuande said, “I wished to protect the people, yet instead I am harming them! I will not enter Xiangyang!” Kongming said, “Jiangling is a vital stronghold of Jingzhou. We should first seize Jiangling as our base.” Xuande said, “That accords perfectly with my wishes.” Thereupon he led the people away from the main road to Xiangyang and set out toward Jiangling. Many people within Xiangyang took advantage of the disorder to flee the city and follow Xuande. Wei Yan and Wen Ping fought from the hour of the Serpent until the hour of the Goat, by which time all their men had fallen. Wei Yan then wheeled his horse and fled. Unable to find Xuande, he went instead to Han Xuan, governor of Changsha.

p.src: Now Xuande traveled with more than a hundred thousand soldiers and civilians, several thousand carts large and small, and countless people bearing loads on poles or packs on their backs. Passing Liu Biao’s tomb, Xuande led all his officers in obeisance before it and tearfully declared, “Your unworthy younger brother Bei, lacking virtue and ability, has failed the weighty trust you placed in me. The guilt is mine alone and has nothing to do with the people. May your heroic spirit look down and save the people of Jingzhou and Xiangyang!” His words were exceedingly sorrowful and earnest, and not one among the soldiers and people failed to shed tears.

p.src: Meanwhile, at Fancheng, Cao Cao sent men across the river to Xiangyang to summon Liu Cong before him. Liu Cong was too frightened to go, so Cai Mao and Zhang Yun asked to make the journey. Wang Wei secretly advised Liu Cong, “Now that you have surrendered and Xuande has fled, Cao Cao is sure to have grown careless and be off his guard. I beg you to muster a picked force, station it at a strategic pass, and strike him there; Cao Cao can be captured. If Cao Cao is captured, your might will shake the realm; vast though the Central Plain is, it can be pacified merely by circulating a proclamation. Such an opportunity is rarely met and must not be lost.”

p.src: Liu Cong repeated his words to Cai Mao. Cai Mao rebuked Wang Wei: “You know nothing of Heaven’s decree! How dare you speak such reckless nonsense?” Wang Wei angrily cursed him: “Traitor who sells his country! I regret only that I cannot devour your flesh alive!” Cai Mao wished to kill him, but Kuai Yue dissuaded him. Cai Mao then went with Zhang Yun to Fancheng, where they paid their respects to Cao Cao. Both their words and expressions were exceedingly obsequious. Cao Cao asked, “How many troops, horses, funds, and provisions does Jingzhou now possess?” Cai Mao replied, “Fifty thousand cavalry, one hundred and fifty thousand infantry, and eighty thousand marines—a total of two hundred and eighty thousand. Most of the funds and provisions are in Jiangling. What remains in the other places is also enough to supply us for a year.” Cao Cao asked, “How many warships are there? And who has been commanding them?” Cai Mao replied, “There are more than seven thousand warships, large and small. The two of us have been in command of them.”

p.src: Cao Cao thereupon made Cai Mao Marquis Who Guards the South and Commander-in-Chief of the Navy, and Zhang Yun Marquis Who Aids Submission and Deputy Commander of the Navy. p.src: Meanwhile, Cai Mao and Zhang Yun returned to Liu Cong and related in full Cao Cao’s promise to recommend that the general should forever govern Jingzhou and Xiangyang. Liu Cong was overjoyed. The next day, he and his mother, Lady Cai, bore the seals, ribbons of office, and military tallies and personally crossed the river to welcome Cao Cao with obeisance. After comforting them, Cao Cao led the officers accompanying his campaign forward and encamped outside Xiangyang. Cai Mao and Zhang Yun ordered the people of Xiangyang to burn incense and bow in welcome. Cao Cao soothed and instructed them all with gracious words. Once seated in the government hall within the city, he immediately summoned Kuai Yue forward and reassured him, saying, “I rejoice not that I have gained Jingzhou, but that I have gained Yidu.” He then appointed Kuai Yue Administrator of Jiangling and Marquis of Fancheng. Fu Xun, Wang Can, and the others were all made Marquises Within the Passes; but Liu Cong was appointed Inspector of Qingzhou and ordered to depart at once.

Cao Cao said, “A truly loyal minister!” He appointed him Administrator of Jiangxia, bestowed on him the rank of Marquis Within the Passes, and ordered him to lead troops and clear the way. By our reckoning, he is just over three hundred li away.” Cao Cao ordered each division to select the finest men, forming five thousand armored cavalry, and advance through the night, with orders to overtake Liu Bei within one day and one night. The main army followed in successive columns.

p.src: It was the end of autumn and the beginning of winter, and the chill wind pierced to the bone; dusk drew near, and cries of lamentation filled the fields. At about the fourth watch, shouts were suddenly heard approaching from the northwest, shaking the earth. Xuande was greatly alarmed. He hastily mounted and led more than two thousand picked troops of his own command to meet the enemy. Cao Cao’s troops swept down upon them with irresistible force. Xuande fought desperately. At the moment of greatest peril, Zhang Fei fortunately arrived with his troops, hewed open a road of blood, and rescued Xuande, fleeing eastward with him. Wen Ping blocked their way at the head of his troops. Xuande cursed him: “Traitor who betrayed his lord! How can you still have the face to show yourself before men?” Wen Ping’s face filled with shame, and he led his troops away to the northeast. Zhang Fei guarded Xuande as they fought and retreated. They fled until daybreak. Only when the shouts gradually faded into the distance did Xuande rein in his horse to rest. Looking over those who had followed him, he found only a little more than a hundred horsemen; the common people and their families, as well as Mi Zhu, Mi Fang, Jian Yong, Zhao Yun, and all the rest, had vanished without a trace. Xuande wept bitterly and said, “More than a hundred thousand living souls have suffered this great calamity because of their devotion to me; and of my generals and family, I know not who lives or who has died. Even a man of earth and wood could not help but grieve!”
